turns.text: Hi Noor, hi Mom. Thanks for keeping the log going. It's short, but I can see the pattern. Can we start with test days?
Sure. Tests are bad. She stayed home for bio, came home early from math and chem, stayed home for English.
Noor, I want to hear your side. What's a test morning like?
I wake up and my stomach is already bad. Like I can't eat. And I keep thinking about what's going to be on it.
And on the days you go in, like chem, what happens?
I sit down and they hand it out and I look at the first question and I just, I can't. So I ask to go to the bathroom and I text my mom.
So you go in, and when it spikes you leave and text Mom. And Mom, you come get her.
Yes. What am I going to do, leave her crying in a bathroom?
That's a very understandable thing to want to stop. Noor, if you picture the test being handed out, how high is the worry on the zero to ten?
Nine. Honestly nine.
Nine. That's very high. What's the worst thing you picture happening?
That I fail. And then my grade drops and then I don't get into any college and everything I did was for nothing.
So one test turns into everything being ruined. That's a big chain for one quiz to carry.
I mean whatever. It's not like it would matter if I wasn't around anyway. Can we talk about something else?
She's been really down about grades. When the quarter grades went up on the portal she was off all night. I didn't ask, I just left her alone.
Okay. Noor, was that night about the grades, or something else?
I don't know. Both. I didn't look at all of them.
Okay, that's fine. We don't have to know yet. Let's look at nights too, because Mom wrote a lot about bedtime. Mom?
Since her dad's surgery in the summer, she comes into our room. Checks on him. Asks if he took his pills. Most nights now she ends up on our floor.
Noor, what's the worry at night?
That he'll get sick again when everyone's asleep. Last time it was at night. And nobody noticed till the morning.
That makes so much sense given what happened. How high is it at bedtime?
Seven.
Seven. And when you check on him and he's okay, what happens to the seven?
It goes down. But then I wake up and I have to check again.
Sorry to interrupt, just letting you know your next family is here early, no rush.
Thanks. Okay, so a couple of things to try this week, and I want us to agree on them. For tests, Noor, the next one is the chem retake Thursday?
Yeah. Thursday.

I'd like you to go in Thursday and stay in the room until you hand it in. It doesn't have to be good. You can write your name and answer one question and hand it in. The goal is staying, not the grade.
What if I can't?

Then you sit with it for ten minutes before you ask to leave. Mom, the part for you: if she texts, you don't come get her unless she's actually sick, like a fever. You can text back one line, something like I know it's hard, you can do it.
Okay. I'll try. I don't love it.
That's fair. And for bedtime, Noor, one check on Dad before you go to bed, and then you sleep in your own room. Mom, no floor this week. Can we try that?
One check.
Yes.

Good. So: Noor stays in the chem retake Thursday until she hands it in, or at least ten minutes before asking to leave. Mom doesn't pick her up unless she's sick and sends one encouraging text. At bedtime, one check on Dad, then her own room, no floor. Keep the log going, Mom, two words is fine.
